name: Anbernic RG Cube
specs: Up to PS2 and Dreamcast with upscaling (some stutter), plus DS and 3DS
bestFor: One device that covers everything from Game Boy to PS2
pros: Square screen suits Game Boy, arcade and DS games without stretching
Hall-effect sticks, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and video out
Comfortable rear grips and a big battery
cons: Square screen is not ideal for widescreen games
Not a vertical Game Boy shape
verdict: The most versatile pick on the list. The square screen sounds like a gimmick, but it makes DS games and arcade shooters genuinely playable while still handling 8- and 16-bit classics cleanly. Reviewers at GamesRadar named it their best retro handheld overall.

name: AYANEO Pocket Air Mini
specs: Up to Dreamcast upscaled; only a handful of PS2 and GameCube games
bestFor: Android flexibility and premium build on a budget
pros: Build quality that feels like a more expensive device
4:3 screen fits retro games well
Hall sticks and analog triggers at this price
cons: Thick around the grips
Limited PS2 and GameCube performance
One reviewer reported visible screen ghosting
verdict: Retro Dodo ranks it first in its list, largely on price-to-quality. It is the cheapest way here to get an Android handheld with proper sticks and triggers. If screen ghosting bothers you, check the return policy and test it early.

name: TRIMUI Brick
specs: Linux (simple stock OS, custom firmware available)
Game Boy through PS1; some N64 and Dreamcast
bestFor: A sleek, pocket-sized handheld that just works
pros: Sharp, bright screen for its size
Swappable shoulder buttons in the box
Easy stock OS and good community support
cons: No analog sticks (D-pad can mimic one)
Small screen and no video out
Can run warm in heavy use
verdict: A tiny, well-designed brick that plays the 8-, 16- and 32-bit libraries well. Retro Catalog named it best budget handheld overall, and Retro Dodo compares the feel to a deck of cards.

name: Anbernic RG35XXSP
specs: HDMI out, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, microSD up to 512GB
pros: Folds shut to protect the screen
Fits a pocket neatly
Far nicer backlit screen than an original GBA SP
cons: Flat D-pad and buttons, like the original SP
Gets warm under load
No PS2 support
verdict: If you want the fold-up shape, this is the easy buy. GamesRadar calls it the best clamshell, and it can play more than GBA games, including PS1 and some Dreamcast.

name: AYN Odin 2
price: Roughly $300–$460, depending on RAM and storage
specs: PS2, GameCube, PSP and everything older; Android games and cloud streaming
bestFor: Someone who wants to play PS2 and GameCube without compromise
pros: Handles PS2 and GameCube with smooth frame rates
Big, sharp 1080p screen
Comfortable shape for long sessions
cons: Expensive and overkill if you only play 8- and 16-bit games
Face buttons are on the small side
verdict: GamesRadar names it the best handheld for PS2, and Retro Dodo calls it close to flawless. It is the splurge pick, and the right one if the person you are shopping for already owns a big retro library.

name: Analogue Pocket
specs: FPGA hardware recreation, not software emulation
Original Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges; adapters add Game Gear, Lynx and Neo Geo Pocket
bestFor: Game Boy collectors who want to use their real cartridges
pros: Superb build quality and a stunning screen
Plays real cartridges with high accuracy
Large community of extra cores
cons: High price
Often sold out, so verify the seller before buying
verdict: Not an emulation handheld in the usual sense, which makes it a distinctive gift for a collector. Reviewers rate it among the finest handhelds for original carts. Stock is inconsistent, so check who is selling it on Amazon.

name: MagicX Zero 40
specs: Nintendo DS and vertical arcade shooters
bestFor: DS fans and arcade shmup players
pros: Tall screen suits DS and vertical shooters
Hall-effect stick and save states
Surprisingly comfortable
cons: Not ideal for every console's aspect ratio
Buttons can feel crunchy
verdict: A niche pick that does its niche well. GamesRadar tested it for a month and liked it for DS games and arcade shooters, with the caveat that a used DS can cost less.

name: Anbernic RG477M
bestFor: A premium-feeling Android handheld with strong PS2 performance
pros: Metal shell and gorgeous display
Comfortable sticks and face buttons
Great PS2 and GameCube performance
cons: Clunky launcher and pre-installed AI apps
Loud fan and clicky shoulder buttons
verdict: The hardware is excellent and the software is the weak spot, according to Retro Dodo. Early coverage calls it the strongest Anbernic Android device so far.

name: Evercade Super Pocket
specs: Pre-installed set (Capcom or Taito editions) plus Evercade cartridges
bestFor: Kids, gamers who hate tinkering and anyone who likes physical cartridges
pros: Pick up and play, with nothing to set up
Officially licensed games
Works with the Evercade cartridge library
cons: You cannot add your own game files
D-pad is not to everyone's taste
verdict: The least fussy gift on this list. It is not a ROM machine, and that is the point: the games are included and the cartridge library keeps growing.

name: Anbernic RG28XX
specs: Mini HDMI out, USB-C controller support, microSD up to 512GB
8- and 16-bit systems and PS1; some Dreamcast
bestFor: A tiny, cheap handheld that fits in any pocket
pros: Truly pocketable, Game Boy Micro style
Good battery life
HDMI out for the TV
cons: Small and a bit cramped
Shoulder buttons rattle
No PS2
verdict: A fun little device for the price. GamesRadar picked it as the best budget retro handheld and notes that it handles PS1 better than you would expect.

name: Anbernic RG35XX Plus
specs: Up to Dreamcast, DS, PS1, some PSP
bestFor: The cheapest solid Game Boy-style handheld
pros: Very affordable
Wi-Fi and a bigger battery than the original RG35XX
Pocket-friendly DMG-style shell
cons: Basic stock OS (custom firmware helps)
Uncomfortable shoulder buttons
verdict: Still a solid starter handheld, though Retro Dodo notes Anbernic has newer alternatives. Good if the budget is tight and you do not mind installing custom firmware.
